domain:
    # N: number of samples (rows in the original C code)
    # M: number of variables (columns in the original C code)
    i: dim in [0, N)          # row index over samples
    j: dim in [0, M)          # column index for per-column stats
    p: dim in [0, M)          # row index in correlation matrix (variable index)
    q: dim in [0, M)          # col index in correlation matrix (variable index)
    k: dim in [0, N)          # reduction index over samples

data:
    # Input data as in the original C code: data[i][j], row-major in j.
    data[i, j]: in  DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * M + j      # row-major: j is unit stride

    # Output correlation matrix corr[p][q], row-major in q.
    corr[p, q]: out DATA_TYPE = (p, q) -> p * M + q      # row-major: q is unit stride

    # Temporary 1D arrays for per-column statistics.
    mean[j]:    tmp DATA_TYPE = j -> j                   # logical 1D, contiguous
    var[j]:     tmp DATA_TYPE = j -> j
    stddev[j]:  tmp DATA_TYPE = j -> j
    scale[j]:   tmp DATA_TYPE = j -> j                  # 1 / (sqrt(float_n) * stddev[j])

parameters:
    float_n: DATA_TYPE         # equal to N (cast to DATA_TYPE)
    eps:     DATA_TYPE         # small threshold, = 0.1
    one:     DATA_TYPE         # constant 1.0

    # Tunable constants for optimization (chosen offline for a given machine).
    T_row: int                 # tile size along the sample dimension (i,k)
    T_col: int                 # tile size along the variable dimensions (j,p,q)
    VEC:   int                 # SIMD vector width along unit-stride dimensions

computation:
    #-----------------------------------------------
    # 1. Column-wise mean: mean[j] = (1/float_n) * sum_i data[i][j]
    #-----------------------------------------------
    mean_pass:
        for j:
            mean[j] = (1.0 / float_n) * sum(i in [0, N), data[i, j])

    #-----------------------------------------------
    # 2. Column-wise variance and stddev:
    #    var[j]   = sum_i (data[i][j] - mean[j])^2
    #    sigma[j] = sqrt(var[j] / float_n)
    #    stddev[j] = (sigma[j] <= eps) ? 1.0 : sigma[j]
    #    scale[j]  = 1 / (sqrt(float_n) * stddev[j])
    #-----------------------------------------------
    var_and_stddev_pass:
        for j:
            var[j] = sum(i in [0, N),
                        let d  = data[i, j] - mean[j] in
                        d * d)

            # Compute sigma and stddev exactly as the Halide code:
            let sigma_j = sqrt(var[j] / float_n) in
            if sigma_j <= eps:
                stddev[j] = one
            else:
                stddev[j] = sigma_j

            # Precompute scaling factor used in normalization:
            # normalized[i][j] = (data[i][j] - mean[j]) / (sqrt(float_n) * stddev[j])
            # => scale[j] = 1 / (sqrt(float_n) * stddev[j]).
            scale[j] = 1.0 / (sqrt(float_n) * stddev[j])

    #-----------------------------------------------
    # 3. Correlation matrix.
    #
    # Use algebra to avoid materializing normalized[i][j]:
    #
    #   normalized[i][j] = (data[i][j] - mean[j]) * scale[j]
    #
    # Correlation off-diagonal (p != q) is:
    #   corr[p][q] = sum_k normalized[k][p] * normalized[k][q]
    #              = scale[p] * scale[q] *
    #                sum_k (data[k][p] - mean[p]) * (data[k][q] - mean[q])
    #
    # Diagonal elements are forced to 1.0 to match the original code.
    # We only compute p < q and mirror to p > q to avoid redundant work.
    #-----------------------------------------------
    corr_diag:
        for p:
            corr[p, p] = one

    corr_offdiag:
        for p:
            for q in [p + 1, M):
                let base = sum(k in [0, N),
                               let dp = data[k, p] - mean[p] in
                               let dq = data[k, q] - mean[q] in
                               dp * dq) in
                let val  = scale[p] * scale[q] * base in
                corr[p, q] = val
                corr[q, p] = val

dependencies:
    # Column statistics must be computed before correlation.
    for j in [0, M):
        mean_pass(j) -> var_and_stddev_pass(j)

    for all p,q in [0, M):
        var_and_stddev_pass(:) -> corr_diag(p)
        var_and_stddev_pass(:) -> corr_offdiag(p, q)

optimization:
    #------------------------------------------------
    # General notes:
    #  - data[i,j] is row-major in j; we vectorize and tile along j/q
    #    to get unit-stride SIMD loads/stores.
    #  - The heavy work is in corr_offdiag; we tile (p,q,k) to improve
    #    cache reuse and parallelize across (p,q) tiles.
    #  - scale[j] and mean[j] are reused many times, so we keep them
    #    in contiguous 1D arrays to maximize spatial locality.
    #------------------------------------------------

    #-----------------------------------------------
    # Stage 1: mean_pass (reductions over i, independent across j)
    #  - Parallelize across columns j.
    #  - Vectorize across j when possible (use VEC to match SIMD width).
    #-----------------------------------------------
    # for j in [0, M): mean[j] = ...
    parallelize(j)           # different columns can be reduced independently
    vectorize(j, VEC)        # process VEC adjacent columns at once when N is large

    #-----------------------------------------------
    # Stage 2: var_and_stddev_pass
    #  - Same structure as mean_pass: reductions over i, independent across j.
    #-----------------------------------------------
    parallelize(j)
    vectorize(j, VEC)

    #-----------------------------------------------
    # Stage 3: corr_diag
    #  - Simple 1D loop over p; negligible cost vs off-diagonal work.
    #  - Optionally vectorize; no need to parallelize.
    #-----------------------------------------------
    vectorize(p, VEC)

    #-----------------------------------------------
    # Stage 4: corr_offdiag
    #
    # We have a 3D iteration space:
    #   p in [0, M)
    #   q in [p+1, M)
    #   k in [0, N)
    #
    # We tile (p,q) for better cache reuse over k, and tile k so that
    # (2D (p,q) tile) × (k tile) fits in cache.
    #
    # The canonical untiled nest is logically:
    #   for p:
    #     for q in [p+1, M):
    #       base = 0
    #       for k:
    #         base += ...
    #       val = scale[p]*scale[q]*base
    #       corr[p,q] = corr[q,p] = val
    #
    # We'll transform it as follows:
    #   block(p, P, T_col)    -- p -> (P, p_in)
    #   block(q, Q, T_col)    -- q -> (Q, q_in)
    #   block(k, K, T_row)    -- k -> (K, k_in)
    #
    # And reorder loops to:
    #   for P:
    #     for Q:
    #       for K:
    #         for p_in, q_in, k_in:
    #           ...
    # So that each (P,Q,K) tile has good locality in data[k, *].
    #-----------------------------------------------

    # Tile correlation matrix in (p,q) and the reduction dimension k.
    block(p, P, T_col)       # P: outer tile index over p
    block(q, Q, T_col)       # Q: outer tile index over q
    block(k, K, T_row)       # K: outer tile index over samples

    # Interchange to get tile-major ordering:
    # Outer: P, Q (tiles of variables)
    # Then:  K   (tile of samples)
    # Inner: p, q, k  (within-tile work)
    interchange(P, K)        # move sample tiles inside (p,q) tiles
    interchange(Q, K)

    # Within tiles, traverse (q) fastest: corr[p,q] is row-major in q,
    # and data[i,j] is row-major in j. This improves spatial locality.
    interchange(q, k)        # ensure k is inner or second-inner within a tile

    # Parallelize across tiles of p (and possibly q).
    parallelize(P)           # distribute correlation rows across cores
    # For very large M, parallelizing Q as well is possible, but beware of oversubscription:
    # parallelize(Q)

    # Vectorize across the unit-stride q dimension within tiles.
    vectorize(q, VEC)

    #-----------------------------------------------
    # Optional: minor optimizations
    #  - Hoist tiles of scale[p], scale[q] and mean[p], mean[q] into
    #    registers within each (P,Q) tile to reduce cache traffic.
    #  - Unroll small inner loops over k_in if T_row is small (e.g. 4–8).
    #-----------------------------------------------
    unroll(k, 4)             # if T_row is small, unroll reduction for ILP

    # Note: No extra full-sized temporary matrix (like normalized[i,j])
    # is materialized; normalization is folded into the correlation
    # computation via scale[p], scale[q]. This keeps memory usage
    # within the original footprint plus O(M) temporaries, well under
    # the allowed 50% overhead, while reducing arithmetic inside the k-loop.

```text
domain:
    # N = number of rows (samples), M = number of columns (variables)
    i: dim in [0, N)        # sample index
    j: dim in [0, M)        # column index
    p: dim in [0, M)        # correlation row index
    q: dim in [0, M)        # correlation column index
    d: dim in [0, M)        # diagonal index

data:
    # Input data: C layout is data[i][j] with j contiguous (row-major).
    data[i, j]: in num_t = (i, j) -> i * M + j

    # Output correlation matrix, same logical layout as PolyBench C:
    # corr[i][j] is corr(i, j), row-major.
    corr[i, j]: out num_t = (i, j) -> i * M + j

    # 1D temporaries (negligible memory vs data):
    mean[j]: temp num_t = (j) -> j        # column means
    var[j]:  temp num_t = (j) -> j        # sum of squared deviations (unnormalized variance)
    gamma[j]: temp num_t = (j) -> j       # 1 / (sqrt(float_n) * stddev[j])

parameters:
    float_n: num_t        # = N, passed as in the C++ code
    eps:     num_t        # epsilon for stddev guard, e.g., 0.1
    one:     num_t        # constant 1.0

    # Tunable kernel parameters (chosen at compile- or run-time for a given machine):
    V_mean:   int         # SIMD width for mean/var passes (e.g., 8)
    TP_corr:  int         # tile size along p for correlation (e.g., 32)
    TQ_corr:  int         # tile size along q for correlation (e.g., 32)
    TI_corr:  int         # tile size along i (samples) for correlation (e.g., 256)
    V_corr:   int         # SIMD width for correlation along q (e.g., 8)
    U_corr:   int         # unroll factor for inner-sample loop in correlation (e.g., 4)

computation:
    # 1) Column means: mean[j] = (1 / float_n) * sum_i data[i][j]
    MEAN:
        for j in [0, M):
            mean[j] = (1.0 / float_n) * sum(i in [0, N), data[i, j])

    # 2) Column variances (unnormalized): var[j] = sum_i (data[i][j] - mean[j])^2
    VAR:
        for j in [0, M):
            var[j] = sum(i in [0, N), (data[i, j] - mean[j])^2)

    # 3) Precompute 1 / (sqrt(float_n) * stddev[j]) with epsilon guard.
    #    This matches:
    #      sigma^2 = var[j] / float_n;
    #      sigma  = sqrt(sigma^2);
    #      if (sigma <= eps) sigma = 1.0;
    #      gamma[j] = 1 / (sqrt(float_n) * sigma);
    GAMMA:
        sqrt_n = sqrt(float_n)
        for j in [0, M):
            sigma2 = var[j] / float_n
            sigma  = sqrt(sigma2)
            if sigma <= eps:
                # stddev forced to 1.0 → gamma = 1 / sqrt_n
                gamma[j] = 1.0 / sqrt_n
            else:
                gamma[j] = 1.0 / (sqrt_n * sigma)

    # 4) Off-diagonal correlations as dot products of normalized columns.
    #    Each normalized value is:
    #      norm(i, j) = (data[i][j] - mean[j]) * gamma[j]
    #    and corr[p][q] (for p != q) is sum_i norm(i, p) * norm(i, q).
    CORR_OFFDIAG:
        for p in [0, M):
            for q in [0, M):
                if p != q:
                    corr[p, q] =
                        sum(i in [0, N),
                            ((data[i, p] - mean[p]) * gamma[p]) *
                            ((data[i, q] - mean[q]) * gamma[q]))

    # 5) Diagonal elements are exactly 1.0 (as in the original C code).
    CORR_DIAG:
        for d in [0, M):
            corr[d, d] = one

optimization:
    # Mean and variance passes (MEAN, VAR, and GAMMA):
    #  - Independent across columns j, so we parallelize there.
    #  - Rows i are contiguous in memory inside each row, so we SIMD-vectorize over i.
    parallelize(j)             # parallelize per-column work (good load balance for large M)
    vectorize(i, V_mean)       # use SIMD for reductions over i when computing mean/var

    # Precompute gamma[j] once per column:
    #  - GAMMA has no inner i loop; hoisting j ensures no redundant work inside correlation.
    hoist(j)                   # gamma[j] fully computed before any use in correlation

    # Correlation kernel (CORR_OFFDIAG, CORR_DIAG):
    # Treat corr = Xᵀ X where X[i,j] = (data[i,j] - mean[j]) * gamma[j].
    # We:
    #   * tile the M×M output into TP_corr×TQ_corr tiles (P, Q).
    #   * tile the sample dimension i into chunks of size TI_corr (I_corr).
    #   * run in outer-product order (iterate over i-tiles outermost) so each normalized row
    #     is reused across many (p,q) pairs.
    #   * parallelize over P (tile rows of the correlation matrix).
    #   * vectorize along q (contiguous dimension) for efficient SIMD FMAs.
    block(p, P, TP_corr)       # p = P * TP_corr + p_inner
    block(q, Q, TQ_corr)       # q = Q * TQ_corr + q_inner
    block(i, I_corr, TI_corr)  # i = I_corr * TI_corr + i_inner

    hoist(I_corr)              # make sample tiles outermost: for I_corr { for P,Q { ... i_inner ... } }
                               # → outer-product style accumulation, improves cache reuse of data[i,*]

    parallelize(P)             # distribute correlation tiles across threads (32-core CPU)
                               # (P×Q space can be further fused if additional parallelism is needed)

    vectorize(q, V_corr)       # inside each tile, SIMD across q_inner (contiguous columns)

    unroll(i, U_corr)          # unroll the small inner i_inner loop to expose ILP in the dot products

    # Symmetry exploitation (optional but recommended):
    #  - corr[p, q] == corr[q, p]; we can restrict computation to p <= q and mirror.
    #  - This halves the arithmetic for the correlation kernel while preserving semantics.
    #  - Expressed logically as:
    #       for P,Q:
    #         for p,q in tile:
    #           if p < q: compute corr[p,q] via sum(...)
    #           if p > q: corr[p,q] = corr[q,p]
    #           if p == q: corr[p,p] = one
    #  - Not shown as a separate 'for' in the computation section to keep the core semantics simple.
```

domain:
    # N: number of rows (samples), M: number of columns (variables)
    i: dim in [0, N)          # sample index used in reductions
    j: dim in [0, M)          # column index for per-column statistics
    p: dim in [0, M)          # row index of correlation matrix
    q: dim in [0, M)          # column index of correlation matrix

data:
    # Input data: C data[i][j], laid out row-major
    data[i, j]: in DATA_TYPE  = (i, j) -> i * M + j

    # Intermediate 1D column-wise statistics
    mean[j]:   temp DATA_TYPE = (j)     -> j          # contiguous
    var[j]:    temp DATA_TYPE = (j)     -> j
    stddev[j]: temp DATA_TYPE = (j)     -> j
    scale[j]:  temp DATA_TYPE = (j)     -> j          # 1 / (sqrt(N) * stddev[j])

    # Output correlation matrix, C corr[p][q], row-major
    corr[p, q]: out DATA_TYPE = (p, q)  -> p * M + q

parameters:
    float_n: DATA_TYPE                 # == (DATA_TYPE) N
    eps:     DATA_TYPE = 0.1           # numerical threshold for stddev
    one:     DATA_TYPE = 1.0

    # Tunable blocking / vector widths (chosen for a modern x64 CPU with wide vectors and LLC)
    TI_stats: int = 256                # tile size along i for statistics loops
    TJ_stats: int = 32                 # tile size along j for statistics loops
    TP_corr:  int = 32                 # tile size along p for corr
    TQ_corr:  int = 32                 # tile size along q for corr
    TI_corr:  int = 256                # tile size along i for corr reduction
    VW:       int = 8                  # vector width along the innermost i-like loop

computation:
    # 1) Column-wise mean:
    #    mean[j] = (1 / float_n) * sum_{i=0..N-1} data[i,j]
    for j:
        mean[j] = 0
        mean[j] += sum(i in [0, N), data[i, j] / float_n)

    # 2) Column-wise variance accumulator (without dividing by float_n yet):
    #    var[j] = sum_{i=0..N-1} (data[i,j] - mean[j])^2
    for j:
        var[j] = 0
        var[j] += sum(i in [0, N),
                      let d = data[i, j] - mean[j] in d * d)

    # 3) Standard deviation with epsilon handling:
    #    sigma[j]   = sqrt(var[j] / float_n)
    #    stddev[j]  = (sigma[j] <= eps) ? 1.0 : sigma[j]
    for j:
        let sigma = sqrt(var[j] / float_n)
        stddev[j] = (sigma <= eps) ? one : sigma

    # 4) Precompute per-column scaling factors to eliminate divisions inside the hot loops:
    #    scale[j] = 1.0 / (sqrt(float_n) * stddev[j])
    #    This turns the per-sample normalization into a pair of multiplies.
    let sqrt_n = sqrt(float_n)
    for j:
        scale[j] = one / (sqrt_n * stddev[j])

    # 5) Correlation matrix:
    #    Using normalized data:
    #        norm[i,j] = (data[i,j] - mean[j]) * scale[j]
    #    the correlation coefficient between columns p and q is:
    #        corr[p,q] = sum_i norm[i,p] * norm[i,q]
    #    We exploit symmetry and compute only the upper triangle, then mirror.
    #    Diagonal is forced to 1.0 to match the original C semantics.
    #
    #    NOTE: norm[i,j] is *not* stored; it is an inline expression.
    for p in [0, M):
        # Diagonal entries
        corr[p, p] = one

        # Strict upper triangle: p < q
        for q in [p + 1, M):
            # Compute the dot product of normalized columns p and q:
            let s = sum(i in [0, N),
                        let np = (data[i, p] - mean[p]) * scale[p] in
                        let nq = (data[i, q] - mean[q]) * scale[q] in
                            np * nq)
            corr[p, q] = s
            corr[q, p] = s      # enforce symmetry, lower triangle

optimization:
    # GENERAL NOTES:
    # - All column-wise statistics (mean, var, stddev, scale) are independent in j
    #   and can be parallelized across columns.
    # - For good cache behavior on row-major data[i,j], we traverse i as outer
    #   and j as inner in the statistics loops (row-major order), *even though*
    #   the mathematical formulation is column-wise.
    # - The correlation computation is O(M^2 * N). We:
    #   * tile p and q to work on submatrices of corr that fit in cache,
    #   * tile i (the reduction dimension) for L1/L2 reuse,
    #   * parallelize across tiles in (p,q),
    #   * inline the normalization (norm) expression, avoiding a large N×M buffer.
    #
    # New directives used below:
    # - inline(name): compute 'name' on-the-fly at its use sites instead of storing
    #   it as a full array.
    # - fuse(D1, D2, F): fuse loops over D1 and D2 into a single loop over F to
    #   improve parallel granularity and avoid nested parallelism.

    # 1) Statistics phase (mean, var, stddev, scale)

    # a) Block and reorder loops for mean/var to traverse data row-major:
    #    Original logical order: for j: for i: ...
    #    Optimized physical order: for i in tiles: for j in tiles-in-row: ...
    block(j, J_stats, TJ_stats)          # j -> (J_stats outer, j inner)
    block(i, I_stats, TI_stats)          # i -> (I_stats outer, i inner)
    interchange(I_stats, J_stats)        # outer: I_stats, then J_stats
    interchange(j, i)                    # inner: j fastest for row-major data

    # b) Parallelize statistics across columns (outer tiled j) and vectorize across i.
    parallelize(J_stats)
    vectorize(i, VW)

    # 2) Correlation phase (corr[p,q])

    # a) Do not materialize the normalized matrix; inline its expression
    #    ( (data[i,j] - mean[j]) * scale[j] ) directly inside the corr reduction.
    inline(scale)        # scale itself is tiny and will live in registers / L1
    # (norm is only an expression, no explicit array to inline)

    # b) Tile the correlation matrix to improve cache locality.
    #    corr[p,q] tiles: size TP_corr × TQ_corr.
    block(p, P, TP_corr)                 # p -> (P outer, p inner)
    block(q, Q, TQ_corr)                 # q -> (Q outer, q inner)

    # c) Tile the reduction over samples i to keep a working set of data in L1/L2.
    block(i, I_corr, TI_corr)            # i -> (I_corr outer, i inner)

    # d) Make tile loops outermost, and the per-tile (p,q,i) loops innermost.
    hoist(P)                             # move P outermost
    hoist(Q)
    hoist(I_corr)

    # e) Fuse tile indices (P,Q) into a single parallel dimension to avoid nested
    #    parallelism and to expose more coarse-grain tasks.
    fuse(P, Q, PQ)                       # PQ ranges over all (P,Q) tiles
    parallelize(PQ)

    # f) Within each tile, iterate i-tiles outer, then p, then q, and make q
    #    the fastest-varying dimension to write corr row-major.
    interchange(I_corr, p)
    interchange(p, q)

    # g) Vectorize the innermost part of the reduction over i. This corresponds
    #    to processing VW samples at a time when accumulating each corr[p,q].
    vectorize(i, VW)

    # h) Unroll very small loops where beneficial: the inner tiles of p and q.
    #    (Assuming TP_corr and TQ_corr are modest, e.g., 16–32.)
    unroll(p, 2)
    unroll(q, 2)

    # i) The diagonal assignment corr[p,p] = 1.0 is bandwidth-light; compute it
    #    in a separate pass over p and parallelize that trivial loop as well.
    parallelize(p)

```text
domain:
    # N: number of samples (rows), from defines.hpp (N)
    # M: number of variables (columns), from correlation.hpp / defines.hpp (M)
    s: dim in [0, N)          # sample index (row)
    v: dim in [0, M)          # variable index (column)
    p: dim in [0, M)          # correlation row index
    q: dim in [0, M)          # correlation column index

data:
    # Input data. We store it column-major by variable v so that
    # scans over samples s for a fixed column are contiguous in memory.
    # This matches the access pattern of mean/stddev/correlation, which
    # always reduce over s for fixed v.
    #
    # C code: data[i][j] with i in [0,N), j in [0,M)
    # Here we model an equivalent layout:
    #   data[v, s] ≈ data[i = s][j = v]
    # Memory layout: (v, s) -> v * N + s  (column-major by variable)
    data[v, s]: in DATA_TYPE = (v, s) -> v * N + s

    # Correlation matrix, M×M, kept in standard row-major form.
    # C code: corr[i][j] with i,j in [0,M)
    # Here: corr[p, q] ≈ corr[i = p][j = q]
    corr[p, q]: out DATA_TYPE = (p, q) -> p * M + q

    # Small 1D temporaries (negligible vs data/corr):
    mean[v]: temp DATA_TYPE     = v -> v      # layout not performance-critical
    stddev[v]: temp DATA_TYPE   = v -> v
    inv_scale[v]: temp DATA_TYPE = v -> v     # 1 / (sqrt(float_n) * stddev[v])

parameters:
    float_n: DATA_TYPE          # equals N at runtime
    eps: DATA_TYPE = 0.1        # epsilon for stddev threshold

    # Tunable blocking and SIMD parameters (compile-time / tuning parameters)
    TS: int                     # tile size over samples s, e.g., 64 or 128
    TP: int                     # tile size over p (corr row blocks), e.g., 32
    TQ: int                     # tile size over q (corr col blocks), e.g., 32
    VEC: int                    # SIMD width along s, e.g., 8 for AVX2 float, 4 for double

computation:
    # 1. Column-wise means:
    #    mean[v] = (1/float_n) * sum_{s=0..N-1} data[v, s]
    #
    #    This is mathematically identical to the original incremental
    #    "mean[j] += data[i][j] / float_n", but has only one division
    #    per column instead of N.
    for v in [0, M):
        sum_data = sum(s in [0, N), data[v, s])
        mean[v] = sum_data / float_n

    # 2. Column-wise standard deviations and scaling factors:
    #
    # Original C (per column j):
    #   stddev[j] = 0;
    #   for (i) stddev[j] += (data[i][j] - mean[j])^2;
    #   stddev[j] /= float_n;
    #   stddev[j] = sqrt(stddev[j]);
    #   stddev[j] = stddev[j] <= eps ? 1.0 : stddev[j];
    #
    # We compute:
    #   var_over_n = (1/float_n) * sum_s (data[v,s] - mean[v])^2
    #   sigma      = sqrt(var_over_n)
    #   std        = (sigma <= eps) ? 1.0 : sigma
    #   inv_scale[v] = 1 / (sqrt(float_n) * std)
    #
    # which yields the same stddev and normalization factor as the Halide
    # pipeline (up to identical floating‑point operations), but again
    # with only one division by float_n per column.
    for v in [0, M):
        var_over_n = (1.0 / float_n) * sum(s in [0, N),
                                           (data[v, s] - mean[v]) * (data[v, s] - mean[v]))
        sigma = sqrt(var_over_n)
        if sigma <= eps:
            std = 1.0
        else:
            std = sigma
        stddev[v] = std
        inv_scale[v] = 1.0 / (sqrt(float_n) * std)

    # 3. Correlation matrix:
    #
    # Normalized data is conceptually:
    #   normalized[v, s] = (data[v, s] - mean[v]) / (sqrt(float_n) * stddev[v])
    #
    # We avoid explicitly materializing normalized[., .] (which would be
    # N×M extra storage) and instead apply the scaling inside the dot-product.
    #
    # Original (using normalized):
    #   corr[i][j] = sum_k normalized[i,k] * normalized[j,k];
    #   corr[i][i] = 1.0;
    #   corr[j][i] = corr[i][j];
    #
    # We exploit symmetry and compute only for q >= p, mirroring to q < p.
    for p in [0, M), q in [0, M):
        if p == q:
            corr[p, q] = 1.0
        if q > p:
            # normalized[v, s] = (data[v,s]-mean[v]) * inv_scale[v]
            corr_val = sum(s in [0, N),
                           (data[p, s] - mean[p]) * inv_scale[p] *
                           (data[q, s] - mean[q]) * inv_scale[q])
            corr[p, q] = corr_val
            corr[q, p] = corr_val

optimization:
    # Data layout:
    #   Store 'data' as column-major by v with samples s contiguous:
    #       addr(data[v,s]) = v * N + s
    #   This makes all reductions over s (for fixed v, p or q) unit-stride,
    #   improving cache and SIMD utilization. (Already encoded in the
    #   affine definition for data above.)

    # 1. Per-column reductions (mean and stddev):
    #    - The columns v are independent, so we parallelize across v.
    #    - Each sum over s is a long linear reduction, ideal for SIMD.
    #
    #    Pseudocode after blocking:
    #      for Vv in [0, ceil(M/64)):
    #        parallel for v in Vv*64 .. <(Vv+1)*64:
    #          sum over s (vectorized) ...
    block(v, Vv, 64)               # tile columns into chunks of up to 64
    parallelize(Vv)                # run different column tiles in parallel
    vectorize(s, VEC)              # SIMD across samples in the inner reduction

    # 2. Correlation computation (Gram matrix F^T * F where F[v,s] is normalized data):
    #
    #    We treat corr[p,q] as a blocked GEMM:
    #        F has shape (M × N), F^T has (N × M),
    #        corr = F * F^T  (M × M).
    #
    #    Use 3D tiling in (p, q, s) similar to optimized GEMM:
    #      for P in [0, ceil(M/TP)):            # outer tiles over p
    #        for Q in [0, ceil(M/TQ)):          # outer tiles over q
    #          for K in [0, ceil(N/TS)):        # tiles over reduction dim s
    #            for p in P-tile:
    #              for q in Q-tile with q >= p:
    #                for s in K-tile (vectorized):
    #                  accumulate partial dot-product
    #
    #    This structure improves locality for:
    #      - 'data[p,s]' across many q in a q‑tile,
    #      - 'data[q,s]' across many p in a p‑tile,
    #      - partial corr[p,q] stays in L1/L2 within a tile.
    block(p, P, TP)                # tile corr row indices p
    block(q, Q, TQ)                # tile corr col indices q
    block(s, S, TS)                # tile reduction over samples s

    # Ensure the loop order inside the tiles follows: P, Q, S, inner-p, inner-q, inner-s.
    # This realizes a standard 3-level blocked GEMM-style traversal:
    interchange(S, P)              # move sample tiles inside p-tiles
    interchange(S, Q)              # then inside q-tiles: P -> Q -> S -> ...

    # Parallelization:
    #   Parallelize over P (row tiles). Depending on M and the hardware,
    #   you may optionally also parallelize Q, but avoid deep nested
    #   parallelism; instead, choose TP and TQ so that #P * #Q ≈ #cores.
    parallelize(P)

    # Vectorization and unrolling for the innermost reduction over s.
    # After 'block(s, S, TS)', 's' is the inner index within a TS-sized tile.
    vectorize(s, VEC)              # SIMD across samples in each reduction tile
    unroll(s, 4)                   # small unroll to reduce loop overhead

    # Symmetry optimization:
    #   The conditional 'if q > p' in the computation avoids redundant
    #   work for the lower triangle. This does not change the result,
    #   since corr is mathematically symmetric, but halves the arithmetic
    #   cost of the outer p,q loops.
```

```text
domain:
    # N: number of rows (samples), M: number of columns (variables)
    i: dim in [0, N)          # sample index for data rows
    j: dim in [0, M)          # variable index for data columns
    p: dim in [0, M)          # row index in correlation matrix
    q: dim in [0, M)          # column index in correlation matrix
    k: dim in [0, N)          # reduction index over samples (dot products)

data:
    # Input data matrix: C layout data[i][j] -> linear index i*M + j (row-major)
    data[i, j]: in DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * M + j

    # Output correlation matrix corr[p][q] stored row-major
    corr[p, q]: out DATA_TYPE = (p, q) -> p * M + q

    # Temporary 1D statistics over columns (variables)
    mean[j]:  temp DATA_TYPE = j -> j                   # contiguous in j
    var[j]:   temp DATA_TYPE = j -> j
    stddev[j]: temp DATA_TYPE = j -> j
    gamma[j]: temp DATA_TYPE = j -> j                   # scaling factor 1/(sqrt(float_n)*stddev[j])

parameters:
    float_n: DATA_TYPE        # equals N, used for averaging and normalization
    eps:     DATA_TYPE        # small positive threshold, e.g., 0.1

    # Tuning parameters (chosen based on cache sizes and SIMD width)
    TILE_J_STATS: int         # tile size for column loops in stats (e.g., 64)
    TILE_P:       int         # tile size for corr rows p (e.g., 32)
    TILE_Q:       int         # tile size for corr cols q (e.g., 32)
    TILE_K:       int         # tile size for sample reduction k (e.g., 64)
    VEC_J_STATS:  int         # SIMD width for stats across j (e.g., 8 for AVX2+float)
    VEC_Q_CORR:   int         # SIMD width for corr across q

computation:
    # 1. Column means: mean[j] = (1/float_n) * sum_i data[i][j]
    MEAN:
        for j:
            mean[j] = (1.0 / float_n) * sum(i, data[i, j])

    # 2. Column variances (unnormalized): var[j] = sum_i (data[i][j] - mean[j])^2
    VAR:
        for j:
            var[j] = sum(i, (data[i, j] - mean[j]) * (data[i, j] - mean[j]))

    # 3. Standard deviations with epsilon handling:
    #    sigma_j = sqrt(var[j] / float_n)
    #    stddev[j] = (sigma_j <= eps) ? 1.0 : sigma_j
    #    gamma[j] = 1 / (sqrt(float_n) * stddev[j])
    STDDEV_AND_GAMMA:
        for j:
            sigma_j  = sqrt(var[j] / float_n)
            stddev[j] = if sigma_j <= eps then 1.0 else sigma_j
            gamma[j]  = 1.0 / (sqrt(float_n) * stddev[j])

    # 4. Conceptual normalization (not necessarily materialized as a separate array):
    #    x̂[i][j] = (data[i][j] - mean[j]) * gamma[j]
    #    We express it as an inline expression used inside correlation computation.
    #    norm(i,j) is a purely functional alias for the normalized value.
    NORM_EXPR:
        norm(i, j) = (data[i, j] - mean[j]) * gamma[j]

    # 5. Correlation matrix:
    #    Diagonal: corr[p][p] = 1
    #    Off-diagonals: corr[p][q] = sum_k norm[k][p] * norm[k][q]
    #    Exploit symmetry: corr[q][p] = corr[p][q]
    CORR:
        # Set diagonal to 1.0 explicitly as in the reference C code.
        for p:
            corr[p, p] = 1.0

        # Compute only upper triangle (p < q), then mirror.
        for p in [0, M):
            for q in [p + 1, M):
                corr[p, q] = sum(k, norm(k, p) * norm(k, q))
                corr[q, p] = corr[p, q]

optimization:
    # ------------------------------------------
    # Column statistics (MEAN, VAR, STDDEV_AND_GAMMA)
    # ------------------------------------------
    # Access pattern goal:
    #   data is row-major (i major, j minor), so we prefer to sweep i
    #   in the outer loop and j in the inner loop when accumulating
    #   over i, to read each row contiguously.
    #
    # We keep the mathematical definition as "sum over i for each j",
    # but implement with loop interchange and tiling for better locality.

    # Tile j (variables) into blocks of TILE_J_STATS to improve cache reuse
    # of mean/var/stddev/gamma arrays and enable coarse-grain parallelism.
    block(j, J_stats, TILE_J_STATS)

    # Interchange loops so that the stats passes scan rows contiguously:
    #   for i in [0,N):
    #     for J_stats:
    #       for j in tile:
    #         ...
    # This minimizes cache misses on row-major data[i][*].
    hoist(i)

    # Parallelize over tiles of columns (J_stats): each thread handles a subset
    # of variables across all samples, avoiding write conflicts since each j
    # is independent in MEAN / VAR / STDDEV_AND_GAMMA.
    parallelize(J_stats)

    # Vectorize across j inside a tile for SIMD. This turns per-row stats into
    # vector loads/stores across adjacent columns.
    vectorize(j, VEC_J_STATS)

    # ------------------------------------------
    # Correlation computation (CORR)
    # ------------------------------------------
    # We use a blocked algorithm over (p,q) and k to:
    #   - exploit symmetry (p<q) to halve the number of pairs,
    #   - reuse each normalized row norm[k,*] while accumulating a tile of corr,
    #   - keep working tiles of corr in L1/L2 cache.

    # Tile correlation rows (p) and columns (q) into rectangular blocks.
    block(p, P, TILE_P)      # outer tile index P, inner p
    block(q, Q, TILE_Q)      # outer tile index Q, inner q

    # Tile reduction over samples k to fit working-set of norm(k,*) into cache.
    block(k, K, TILE_K)

    # Reorder so that the outermost loops iterate over (P,Q) tiles,
    # then over K-tiles, then within tiles over (p,q):
    #   for P in [0, ceil(M/TILE_P)):
    #     parallel over P
    #       for Q in [0, ceil(M/TILE_Q)):
    #         for K in [0, ceil(N/TILE_K)):
    #           for p in tile P:
    #             for q in tile Q (with q > p when in upper triangle):
    #               accumulate over k in that K-tile
    hoist(P)
    hoist(Q)

    # Parallelize correlation tiles across P (row-tile index). This gives
    # coarse-grain parallelism with minimal synchronization, since distinct
    # P-tiles write to disjoint row ranges in corr.
    parallelize(P)

    # Inside each tile, vectorize across q to exploit SIMD when updating
    # multiple corr[p, q] with the same p and current k.
    vectorize(q, VEC_Q_CORR)

    # Unroll part of the reduction over K to expose instruction-level
    # parallelism and amortize loop overhead; TILE_K is tuned such that
    # K * unroll_factor fits well in L1/L2 cache.
    unroll(K, 4)

    # ------------------------------------------
    # Fusion of normalization with correlation
    # ------------------------------------------
    # Instead of materializing norm[i,j] as a full N×M array, compute it
    # on-the-fly inside the correlation kernel to reduce memory footprint
    # and bandwidth. This does *not* change the arithmetic formula:
    #
    #   norm(k, p) = (data[k, p] - mean[p]) * gamma[p]
    #
    # Fusing reduces extra passes over data and avoids an N×M temporary.
    #
    # We define a custom optimization:
    #
    #   fuse(NORM_EXPR, CORR, k)
    #
    # semantics:
    #   - Inline norm(k, p) and norm(k, q) into the CORR computation,
    #     i.e. compute (data[k,p]-mean[p])*gamma[p] and
    #     (data[k,q]-mean[q])*gamma[q] directly in the innermost loops.
    #   - Do not allocate a separate norm[][] buffer.
    #
    # This preserves the mathematical definition of corr[p,q] while
    # minimizing memory traffic and keeping the working set smaller.
    fuse(NORM_EXPR, CORR, k)

    # ------------------------------------------
    # Use of symmetry
    # ------------------------------------------
    # We already restricted the computation domain in CORR (p,q) to p<q
    # and explicitly mirror corr[p,q] into corr[q,p]. This reduces
    # arithmetic by ~2× for the correlation matrix while preserving
    # exact semantics of the original (corr is symmetric with diag 1).
    #
    # No extra directive is needed here, but it is a key semantic
    # optimization expressed in the computation section.
```
